abstract_sentences.text: Classifying protein topology is essential for deciphering biological function, but progress is held back by the lack of large-scale benchmarks that avoid duplicates and by models that do not scale well.
We introduce TEDBench, a large-scale, non-redundant benchmark for protein fold classification constructed from the Encyclopedia of Domains (TED) and Foldseek-clustered AlphaFold structures.
We show that on TEDBench, current protein representation learning methods either require very large models or fail to deliver strong performance.
To address this challenge, we propose Masked Invariant Autoencoders (MiAE), a self-supervised framework for protein structure representation learning.
MiAE uses an extremely high masking ratio of up to 90% with an SE(3)-invariant encoder and a lightweight decoder that reconstructs backbone coordinates from the latent representation and mask tokens.
MiAE scales well and outperforms supervised counterparts and state-of-the-art baselines on TEDBench, establishing a strong recipe for protein fold classification.
To test transfer beyond AlphaFold structures, we further benchmark on a curated dataset from experimental structures of CATH v4.4.

introduction_moves.previous_problem: None; opens with the scale of predicted structures.
introduction_moves.current_answer: AlphaFold-scale data creates an ImageNet-like opportunity, but structural biology lacks a comparable supervised benchmark.
introduction_moves.next_hook: Identify a stable structural unit and label hierarchy.

introduction_moves.previous_problem: What should be the supervised target?
introduction_moves.current_answer: Use protein domains as modular units and CATH as a nested structural taxonomy; formulate topology prediction.
introduction_moves.next_hook: Explain why large-scale labels were previously difficult.

introduction_moves.previous_problem: Why was the objective not already available at scale?
introduction_moves.current_answer: TED combines domain segmentation and structure-based matching to make AFDB annotation feasible.
introduction_moves.next_hook: Turn TED annotations into a benchmark with an unambiguous label.

introduction_moves.previous_problem: How can TED become a standard task?
introduction_moves.current_answer: TEDBench assigns the largest domain CATH T-level label and projects TED onto Foldseek-clustered AFDB with an experimental external test.
introduction_moves.next_hook: Quantify scale and compare with existing benchmarks.

introduction_moves.previous_problem: Is the benchmark large enough to discriminate methods?
introduction_moves.current_answer: Give 462,175 predicted structures, 27,638 experimental structures, and a >30x comparison with prior fold datasets.

introduction_moves.previous_problem: Can existing representation learners scale to TEDBench?
introduction_moves.current_answer: GotenNet reaches only 65.44 external macro-F1 and several pretrained models are weak under linear probing; MiAE is proposed with high masking and asymmetric decoding.
introduction_moves.next_hook: State quantitative headline results and contributions.

introduction_moves.previous_problem: Is MiAE more than an architecture proposal?
introduction_moves.current_answer: Preview +10.23 macro-F1 from scratch, 70.44 linear-probing macro-F1, fewer parameters, and experimental-structure transfer; list four contributions.

final_judgment.single_storyline: The paper first turns protein fold classification into a large, non-redundant, single-target benchmark with an independent experimental test, then uses MiAE residue frames, extreme masking and an asymmetric encoder-decoder to learn structure-centric representations; the same TEDBench supports baseline, transfer, scale and component diagnosis. [pp. 1-9, §§1-5, explicit/interpretation]
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: The main body keeps TED/Foldseek construction, pLDDT and label/split rules, MiAE frame-mask-encoder-decoder mechanism, Table 2-3 headline comparisons, Figure 4-6 trends, and explicit Limitations. [pp. 3-9, explicit: “Macro F1 ... primary metric”; “This work has several limitations”]
final_judgment.appendix_moves: Appendix A-C move label code, geometric-attention simplifications, exact five-term loss, dimensions and hyperparameters, baseline provenance, GPU-hour accounting, complete ablations and extra visualizations. This preserves headline readability but leaves label-threshold reproducibility and run-level stability unresolved. [pp. 13-19, explicit/layout observation]
final_judgment.best_pattern: Figure 1 makes data/task/long-tail structure visible before Figure 3 explains the model pipeline; Table 2-3 then place protocol, parameter size and external transfer beside F1, followed by targeted ablations. [pp. 3-9, interpretation grounded in figure/table captions]
final_judgment.largest_gap: The main numerical comparisons are single point estimates without seeds or uncertainty, the model/data/compute comparisons are not fully matched, qualitative t-SNE/attention has no companion metric, and Appendix A defaults to a label threshold different from Section 3.2. [pp. 4, 6-9, 13-14, 17]
final_judgment.transfer_rule: For a large-scale representation paper, freeze deduplication, label denominator, split and independent external source first; then map each architecture choice to a targeted removal/sensitivity control, report the decision-relevant metric with parameter/protocol context, and move reproducibility details to an explicitly called appendix.
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: The rule requires stable provenance for label maps, thresholds, model sizes, pretraining corpus and external test; it cannot turn a single-domain F1 point estimate into general function prediction, domain detection, low-resource deployment or dual-use impact evidence. [pp. 4, 6, 9, 13-17]
final_judgment.evidence: Key evidence: Figure 1 p.3; Figure 3 p.5; Limitations p.9.
